analysis.one_liner: Pauses debt collections, evictions, utility shutoffs, and repossessions during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to stop creditors and debt collectors from garnishing wages, seizing bank accounts, repossessing cars, evicting people for nonpayment, or shutting off utilities during the COVID-19 emergency and for 120 days after it ended. It also barred penalty fees and interest-rate hikes triggered by nonpayment during that window, required extended repayment plans afterward, and created automatic forbearance for anyone who said they had a COVID-related hardship. To soften the blow, it directed the Federal Reserve to set up a low-cost loan facility, paid for with leftover CARES Act money, to cover creditors' documented forbearance losses.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with past-due debts during the pandemic: workers facing wage garnishment, renters facing eviction, households facing utility shutoffs, and car owners facing repossession. Anyone who could attest to a COVID-related hardship could get forbearance without documentation or fees, and after the pause creditors would have to offer stretched-out repayment plans.

how_it_helps.text: During the emergency period and 120 days after, debt collectors could not repossess property, garnish wages, seize bank accounts or benefits, evict someone for nonpayment, or cut off electricity, gas, water, telecom, or sewer service.

Creditors could not add penalty fees or higher interest rates triggered by nonpayment during the covered period, and had to offer extended repayment periods after it ended, ranging from 12 to 36 months depending on the balance owed.

Consumers could get forbearance simply by attesting to a COVID-related financial hardship, with no documentation and no fees or penalties, and violations carried damages at ten times the normal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act amounts.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors and debt collectors, who would have to wait to collect and could not profit from penalty fees during the pause. Taxpayers indirectly back the relief, since the Federal Reserve loan facility compensating creditors for forbearance losses would be funded with CARES Act money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Creditors, debt collectors, and indirectly taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill compensates creditors for forbearance losses through a Federal Reserve loan facility using CARES Act funds, so part of the consumer relief would be financed by public money, and the bill excludes debts from credit agreements made after enactment, letting new lending escape the protections.
It does not cover federally backed mortgage loans, which were already subject to CARES Act forbearance rules, leaving the pause aimed at other consumer debts only.
A blanket halt to evictions and collections, even temporary, puts landlords and small creditors at risk of uncompensated losses on the debts they are owed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit, stopping garnishments, evictions, shutoffs, and repossessions during a nationwide emergency, is large and immediate for households that lost income. The design is generous to creditors, who are reimbursed for forbearance losses from a public credit facility and can escape the rules by writing new credit agreements, which keeps the cost to the industry modest and shifts some of it to taxpayers. The main honest objection is the temporary eviction ban's effect on landlords, though the bill's creditor-compensation facility may reach them as well.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joyce Beatty introduced the bill with Rep. Maxine Waters on July 27, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
It had one cosponsor and no further action of any kind was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors and debt collectors came out ahead: no pause on collections, garnishments, evictions, or utility shutoffs ever took effect, and no extended repayment or automatic forbearance obligations were imposed. Households behind on bills during the pandemic got no federal relief from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats were attached to the bill and no Republican supported it, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the full chamber was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped their ability to garnish wages, seize assets, repossess, and charge penalty fees during the emergency, but a Federal Reserve loan facility funded with CARES Act money would reimburse documented forbearance losses, leaving them largely held harmless on the financial side. Because the bill's consumer benefit depends on restricting collection tactics these firms profit from, their interest runs against the public's in this bill.

The bill bars evicting a consumer for nonpayment during the covered period, delaying rent recovery. As creditors owed payment, they could potentially seek compensation through the bill's Federal Reserve forbearance facility.

The bill bars disconnecting electricity, gas, water, sewer, or broadband service for nonpayment during the covered period, which prevents shutoffs but leaves unpaid bills to accumulate for later repayment plans.
